summary: Psalm 59 begins with a plea for rescue from enemies who are watching for the speaker’s life. The poem moves between descriptions of prowling, violent opponents and confidence that God is a high tower. It ends with the enemies still pictured as wandering at evening, while the speaker resolves to sing of God’s strength and mercy in the morning.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how the Psalter gives words for fear, accusation, anger, and trust in the same prayer. Its heading links it with David and Saul, but psalm headings are ancient evidence whose exact historical force is debated.

context.author: Psalms is a many-writer anthology. This psalm’s heading says it is “A poem by David,” but the wider Psalter’s Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, collection, or reception.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 59 is uncertain.
context.setting: The heading connects the poem with Saul sending men to watch David’s house to kill him. The poem itself speaks from danger, watched by enemies, and repeatedly contrasts night threat with God as refuge.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a heading, repeated imagery, lament, petition for judgment, confidence, and praise.

outline.heading: Cry for rescue
outline.note: The speaker asks God to deliver him from enemies, workers of iniquity, and bloodthirsty men.

outline.heading: Watched without cause
outline.note: The attackers lie in wait, while the speaker denies wrongdoing and asks Yahweh God of Armies to rise and punish wicked traitors.

outline.heading: Enemies at evening
outline.note: The enemies are pictured as dogs prowling the city, speaking violence, while Yahweh laughs and scoffs at them.

outline.heading: God as high tower
outline.note: The speaker turns from threat to waiting for God, calling God his Strength, high tower, and the one who goes before him with loving kindness.

outline.heading: Judgment that teaches
outline.note: The prayer asks God not simply to kill the enemies, but to scatter, bring down, catch, and consume them so that God’s rule is known.

outline.heading: Night hunger, morning song
outline.note: The enemies return and wander unsatisfied, but the speaker sings of God’s strength, loving kindness, refuge, and mercy.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A poem by David, when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him. Deliver me from my enemies, my God. Set me on high from those who rise up against me.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the performance heading, the David-and-Saul setting named in the heading, and the main plea for rescue.

keyVerses.text: Oh, my Strength, I watch for you, for God is my high tower.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns the poem from danger toward trust and introduces the refuge image repeated at the end.

keyVerses.text: Consume them in wrath. Consume them, and they will be no more. Let them know that God rules in Jacob, to the ends of the earth. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm’s hard prayer for judgment and states the desired public recognition of God’s rule.

keyVerses.text: But I will sing of your strength. Yes, I will sing aloud of your loving kindness in the morning. For you have been my high tower, a refuge in the day of my distress.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the final contrast between the enemies’ night wandering and the speaker’s morning praise.

themes: God as high tower and refuge

questions.question: What situation does the heading describe?
questions.answer: The heading says this is a poem connected with David “when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him.” The chapter itself does not narrate the episode; it gives the prayer of someone under threat. Readers differ on how much historical detail a psalm heading proves, so it should be treated as ancient guidance without turning the poem into a full biography.

questions.question: Who are the enemies in this psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm calls them “my enemies,” “those who rise up against me,” “workers of iniquity,” “bloodthirsty men,” “mighty,” and “wicked traitors.” They lie in wait, gather against the speaker, speak curses and lies, and prowl around the city. The text gives their actions and labels, but it does not name individual people beyond the heading’s reference to Saul.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears after the judgment requests in verses 5 and 13. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is no longer known. It signals the psalm’s performance world, but readers should not pretend certainty about its precise function.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say the attack is not because of his own sin?
questions.answer: The speaker says the enemies gather “not for my disobedience, nor for my sin” and adds, “I have done no wrong.” Within the poem, that claim supports the plea for God to rise, behold, and help. It is a claim made in this prayer, not a general claim that the speaker is sinless in every possible sense.

questions.question: Why are the enemies compared to dogs?
questions.answer: The psalm twice pictures them returning at evening, howling like dogs, and going around the city. The image emphasizes restless, threatening movement at night. Verse 15 extends the image by portraying them wandering for food and remaining unsatisfied.

questions.question: What is difficult about the prayers for judgment?
questions.answer: The psalm asks God to punish, scatter, bring down, catch, and consume the enemies. Those requests are severe, and readers differ over how to use such prayers: some stress that the speaker hands judgment to God rather than taking revenge, while others emphasize the moral difficulty of asking for destruction. The chapter itself presents the cry as part of honest prayer under threat, not as a simple command for later readers to imitate directly.

questions.question: Why does verse 11 say, “Don’t kill them”?
questions.answer: The speaker asks that the enemies not be killed immediately, “or my people may forget.” Instead, he asks God to scatter them and bring them down. The prayer seems to imagine judgment that becomes a remembered public lesson, though the text does not explain exactly how that would work.

questions.question: What does the psalm mean by calling God a “high tower”?
questions.answer: “High tower” is the psalm’s image for safety above danger. The speaker uses it while waiting for God in verse 9, then says in verse 16 that God has been his high tower and refuge in distress. The image fits the chapter’s movement from being watched and surrounded to being lifted beyond the reach of attackers.

questions.question: How does the ending change the mood of the psalm?
questions.answer: The enemies are still pictured as returning at evening and wandering unsatisfied. But the speaker’s focus changes to singing in the morning about God’s strength, loving kindness, refuge, and mercy. The psalm does not end by narrating the enemies’ defeat; it ends with resolved praise in the middle of distress.

glossary.def: A term in the heading that points to the psalm’s use in a musical or worship setting, though the exact ancient performance details remain uncertain.
The tune named in the heading. The words are preserved, but the ancient melody is no longer known.
The psalm’s description of violent enemies from whom the speaker asks to be saved.
An uncertain musical or performance marker preserved in the psalm.
The psalm’s repeated image for God as a place of protection and refuge.
A phrase used for God’s loyal mercy or kindness in verses 10 and 16, where the speaker trusts and then praises God.
